newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam gives economy mixed bill of health.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam gives economy mixed bill of health.

text.p: Vietnam's Minister of Planning and Investment said on Sunday the economy had enjoyed another year of vigorous growth in 1996 but faced an array of new and dangerous problems, not least of which was a yawning trade gap.
"In our review of the socio-economic situation for 1996 we can say that besides our achievements, there remain unresolved problems," Tran Xuan Gia wrote in the Vietnam Investment Review.
Gia, editor-in-chief of the weekly, said gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 9.5 percent in 1996 compared with an average of 8.2 percent in the period from 1991 to 1995.

Agricultural output growth was at the top end of a 4.5-4.8 percent government target despite a knock from heavy flooding and other natural disasters, while industry shrugged off a mid-year slowdown to increase its output by 14 percent.
The country's annual inflation rate ended the year at 4.5 percent, its lowest level in decades and a sharp drop from 12.7 percent at the end of 1995.
However, Gia said the communist country's move to deepen its process of reforms along market lines had spawned more complicated problems at both macroeconomic and microeconomic levels.
He pointed to the rapid widening of trade and current account gaps, largely the result of a voracious appetite for imports of capital and, increasingly, consumer goods.
The government has forecast a 1996 trade gap of around $4.0 billion, equivalent to around 18 percent of GDP, compared with $2.3 billion in 1995.
"If this is not solved, it will lead to the collapse of our trade and payment balance in coming years," Gia said, adding that import management was slack and illegal imports still a serious problem.

He said local industry faced a problem of competitiveness as Vietnam integrated deeper into the regional and global economies and said many of the country's approximately 6,000 state-owned companies were operating at a loss.
According to a report in the Thanh Nien newspaper last week, more than half of 4,000 local-level state-owned enterprises are unprofitable and thousands are short of cash.
